title: Winter Sleep (2014) went totally under my radar

commenti.body:
I don’t think Nuri Bilge Ceylan gets enough recognition in US.Recently attended to About Dry Grasses screening in LA and it was mostly Turkish people and not many American viewers.
You should definitely see Once Upon a Time in Anatolia.
Nuri Bilge is one of my favorite directors and i have seen his films hundreds of times.

>About Dry Grasses

How is it? I'm so excited for this to release
I only seen it once and i was mesmerized.Cant wait to watch it on Blu-ray again.Im sure it ll come out from Criterion Janus contemporaries.

I'm yet to see Winter Sleep but it's on my list. Once Upon A Time In Anatolia is superb. The atmosphere is really immersive and the storytelling is subtle - a million miles away from the piledriver approach of a lot of English language films, where the concept of a story "beat" makes perfect sense in that those beats are practically drummed into your skull!

You are in for a treat going through nuri bilge ceylans work. For my money he’s the finest living auteur we have. His work is so profoundly written, but on top of that the pacing and quality of his actual film making is sublime.

In my opinion once upon a time in anatolia is his finest work but they all are excellent. I’m still waiting for a uk release of about dry grasses.

Its such a profound and hauntingly beautiful film. Incredibly subtle as well as you say. It all has this dreamlike quality which makes sense if you’ve ever had your stay up all night yourself before. 

The dynamic between the doctor and prosecutor is one of my favourite in any film

I love this film too. I speak Turkish (as a 1st gen Turkish American) but I still use the subtitles because a lot of the philosophical language goes over my head.

It is heavy, poignant, and slow paced, but the  characters and situations are captivating.

"Dreamlike" is a great word for it. That's a quality I love in films. Tarkovsky, Bunuel, Lynch, Kieslowski, even Kiarostami (in Close Up, say) all have their different ways of being dreamlike in their approaches to storytelling, but each director somehow knows how to make a story "unfold" in ways that are as unpredictable yet uncannily logical as a dream.

I *would* call it a masterpiece. I saw it last year on DVD, and it immediately went on my (sad) little best films list (good news for 2014 as up till then it was looking sadly under-represented). Like you, as soon as it ended I immediately wanted to watch it again, and I did a couple of days later. 

The stand out elements of this film, for me, were the depiction of the environment and the deep, detailed, expertly portrayed character work. And when those two elements were brought together, I felt there was a kind of magic about it. 

When I say environment, I don't just mean the stunning photography of rural Turkey. The interiors too were full of life - full of atmosphere. There was such a real, immediate sense of the world - almost as if you were there. And the characters, their relationships, their psychology and emotional lives - it was all so *real*. I honestly don't think I've seen a film where the complexities and contradictions of human relations has been more closely portrayed. I remember thinking - This is how people are! 

Of course we have to thank Chekhov, on whose writing the film is partly based, for some of that. It's strange to say, because it wasn't purely an adaptation of Chekhov, but this film is the finest interpretation of some Chekhovian archetypes (mostly bored landowners) I've ever seen. 

Soon after I saw the film I saw Ceylan's 2018 The Wild Pear Tree. Although I did not connect with this film so strongly (and was also a little disconcerted by how much it owed to Kiarostami), I still found a huge amount to admire - passages of confident, grand film making. In my opinion, Ceylan is a great film maker.

Yeah, I'd probably call it a masterpiece, it's pretty much flawless anyway. It's my favorite film since Mulholland Drive, and there aren't too many films I haven't seen yet that can take it's place. The main criticism I've heard is that it's too much like a play and not enough cinema. I always have a hard time putting together my thoughts on such issues. Yes, 90% is just people talking, but there are several locations, great acting and so on that elevates it to a great film.

Ceylan's films are always informed by the tensions between East vs West, and urban vs rural. Turkey is a country that took over the legacy of the Ottomans and paid its debts, but positioned itself in opposition to that legacy as a Western secular democracy. 

The film is a great critique of the Turkish intellectual, who originates from Anatolia and claims to know everything about its ordinary people, and is yet so completely disconnected from them. He originates from amongst them and yet he has nothing but disdain for them. This is emphasised in so many scenes, those that I can remember now are the way Aydın stares at the villager's muddy shoes and the way he forces the kid to kiss his hand. 

Ceylan makes this all the more clear by naming the main character Aydın, which means intellectual/enlightened in Turkish.

He and Zeki Demirkubuz, another Turkish director, have an interesting situation going on, they are roasting each other in their films.  


I started liking NBC's films after Once Upon a Time in Anatolia. He has very basic stories, very realistic but his storytelling is very impressive

Yes - I hadn't put this into words specifically, but you're right there's absolutely that tension all the way through the film. Aydin doesn't approve of his wife's altruism, and maybe it's because he doesn't really believe the common people can be helped. He doesn't think they have the sense to pull themselves out of poverty. The irony is, of course, that his wife's charity really does backfire. The man she decides to help turns out to be self destructive and full of bitterness.

To me it was a bit all over the place. There were a lot of characters and plot threads that didn't tie together well enough in my opinion. And it had a lot of plot for it's runtime. With a 3h17m runtime it gets pretty exhausting, I didn't find it as contemplative as a film by Bela Tarr or Weerasethakul so I could feel the time ticking

One could definitely make a good argument about him being the greatest living director right now.

I think what Nuri Bilge Ceylan stated once is something that many films and most notably American films need to learn from, in relation to film conventions. American films always have to tie everything off in a nice bow, we can thank Spielberg for this. Not only this, they often involve "neatly packaged lessons", Nuri said "They want a life coach, I’m just trying to show life as I feel it.”

He understands the human condition, and that's why his films are infinitely interesting.
I went on a Nuri Bilge binge after Winter Sleep. I loved The Wild Pear Tree (which I had seen when it came out) but didn’t like or rate Once Upon A Time…
